reading.synopsis: Lori, a young Boston-raised wife transplanted to rural Vermont, is summoned by a dead leaf tapping at her window, which she tucks against her skin with an almost erotic charge. Over her farmer husband Steve's reluctant permission, she climbs to an abandoned, rock-poor orchard on a ruined farm, where every tree has died except one ancient apple tree, still bearing a few withered fruit. Lori tells the tree this will be her last visit — Steve has forbidden further trips — and the tree responds with animate menace, its branches lashing out and catching her before releasing her. Fleeing down the hillside, she picks up a small dried apple that has rolled free and eats it on the way home. That night she dies suddenly and horribly of a ruptured appendix; the doctor, driving away afterward, asks almost as an afterthought whether she might have swallowed something unusual. Months later, visiting her grave, Steve and his father Ed find a young, vigorous apple tree has sprung up over the grave, its fruit already ripening red in early spring — the same red, Steve realizes aloud, as Lori's cheeks when she used to come back flushed from her climbs to the orchard.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the summons and the climb, the confrontation at the tree and Lori's death, the graveside epilogue
movements: A leaf taps at Lori's window; she leaves her husband and father-in-law's company to make what she promises will be her final visit to a ruined orchard's one living tree.

At the tree, Lori announces she won't return; the tree responds violently, and she flees, unknowingly carrying home and eating one of its dried apples, then dies suddenly that same night of a ruptured appendix.

Months later, at Lori's grave, Steve and Ed discover a young apple tree has grown there, already bearing fruit red as her living cheeks, leaving unstated but unmistakable the implication that something of the orchard tree, or of her, has taken root.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Lori for the climb and confrontation, then to Steve for the graveside epilogue, so the reader witnesses both the seduction and the aftermath without either character ever learning the full shape of what happened to the other.
structure.central_device: A folk-horror vegetal entity whose relationship to Lori is never named as romantic, malevolent, or simply natural, so that her death by a swallowed apple seed reads simultaneously as tragic medical accident and as a consummated claim by something that considered her its own.

characters.name: Lori
characters.note: Explicitly out of place among 'Vermont men and their slow, deliberate way,' her attraction to the tree is charged in openly sensual terms (the leaf 'tingled' against her skin, she feels 'wanted') that the story never reduces to simple explanation.

characters.name: Steve
characters.note: His question to the doctor — 'if we had called you earlier' — and his later recognition of the graveside tree's red fruit as Lori's own remembered blush are the story's two moments of a grief that can sense something is wrong without being able to name it.

characters.name: Ed Patterson
characters.note: The practical, unmoved farmer whose 'graveyards always made him uncomfortable' understates the story's uncanny final image, letting Steve alone register its full weight.

characters.name: The apple tree
characters.note: The only living thing among 'row after row of dead trees,' its motive—love, hunger, territorial anger, or something without a human name at all—is never clarified, and its reappearance transplanted to Lori's grave is the story's only definitive claim about what it was.

settings.name: The abandoned Rickley orchard
settings.note: Poor, rocky soil that 'never yielded a damn thing' for its human owners, yet sustains one impossibly persistent tree — established early, by Ed's own account, as ground that resists ordinary cultivation.

settings.name: The graveyard
settings.note: The story's final setting transplants the orchard's uncanny fertility onto Lori's grave itself, closing the story on an image of growth rather than loss.

motifs: A natural object (a leaf, then a tree) exerting an erotically-charged, quasi-sentient pull on a woman dissatisfied with her human marriage
Barren, rock-poor ground that nonetheless sustains one persistent, unnatural fertility
A death by ordinary medical cause (a ruptured appendix) left open to a supernatural reading by what she swallowed just beforehand
A final image of new growth over a grave that answers the story's central ambiguity without ever stating it outright
A recurring color (red) linking Lori's living blush to the tree's ripening fruit
reading.significance: The story sits in a mode closer to New England folk-horror or a modernized version of a fertility myth than to Dick's more familiar science-fictional material — there is no technology, no future setting, only a woman drawn to something old and half-alive in the landscape. Its power comes from consistently declining to state what the tree is or wants: Lori's death could be read purely clinically (a burst appendix, worsened by rural distance from a hospital, exactly as Steve bitterly notes), or as the tree completing a claim on her that began the moment the leaf first tapped at her window. The final image — a vigorous young tree already fruiting over her grave, its apples the same red as her living cheeks — refuses to let the clinical reading stand alone without also insisting on the other one.
reading.closing_note: Ed's flat, uneasy 'Come on. Let's get out of here' closes the story on unresolved dread rather than explanation, exactly mirroring the tree's own silence throughout Lori's visits to it.

distinctive_terms.label: Father
distinctive_terms.note: Ed Patterson's role as father-in-law frames the story's second, graveside movement.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a near-sentient natural force outside ordinary human categories, worshipped and feared in near-ritual visits, that ultimately claims a devotee's life and body
Lori's charged, secretive visits to the tree function as a kind of infidelity to her marriage, one the story frames in openly desirous rather than merely curious terms

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick names this story (as 'Withered Apples') in the same Exegesis list as 'Beyond the Door,' cited immediately after his claim that only what comes in 'from outside' an illusory, self-generated world is genuinely real. A second Exegesis hit is excluded here as a bare index/bibliography entry with no interpretive content.

evidence.source: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "Martians Come in Clouds" "The Eyes Have It" "Beyond the Door" "Withered Apples" "Not by Its Cover"
evidence.reading: Grouped with four other early minor stories (including 'Beyond the Door,' also read in this project) as material Dick returned to decades later in support of his gnostic claim that reality only truly breaks in 'from outside' an illusory world — here, that intrusion would presumably be the tree itself, an animate, desiring force from outside the ordinary rural world Lori otherwise inhabits.

open_questions: What does footnote 95 attached to the five-story Exegesis list actually say? It may state directly what Dick saw in this story as an instance of 'the real breaking in from outside.'

Is there any biographical basis for this story's rural-Vermont setting and its Boston-versus-country class tension, given Dick's own residence in Point Reyes Station and rural Marin County by the time of writing?
Is there secondary criticism reading this story alongside Dick's other treatments of predatory or claiming female/natural forces, or is its folk-horror mode considered an outlier in his corpus?
